title: Database Indexing Trade-offs under High Write Volume
subtitle: B-Tree Fill Factor Tuning, Write Amplification Elimination & Covering Indexes
problem_statement: A financial transaction ingestion table handles 4,000 writes/sec and 200 reads/sec. Developers added 8 different indexes on the table to speed up ad-hoc operational queries. As a result, disk write IOPS spiked 7x, WAL generation overloaded replication, and insert latency degraded from 2ms to 45ms.

faded_bug.description: Low-cardinality and overlapping indexes multiplying write amplification on every insert.

invariants.description: P99 insert latency must remain below 15ms under 4000 writes/sec.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Walk through what PostgreSQL's storage engine does on disk when a row is inserted into a table with 8 B-Tree indexes.
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: If random UUIDv4 keys are used as the primary key, why does write throughput collapse once the table size exceeds available RAM?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: We must support query by `status = 'PENDING'` (which is 0.1% of rows) and `created_at`. How do you index this with zero write amplification on completed rows?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: Cloud provider disk IOPS limits are exceeded. How do you tune PostgreSQL fillfactor and HOT (Heap-Only Tuples) updates to reduce page splits?

counter_probes.counter_question: Status has only 4 distinct values: PENDING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED. Why will the PostgreSQL query planner ignore a standard B-Tree index on status for 99% of queries?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: B-Tree indexes on low-cardinality columns have poor selectivity; a sequential scan or bitmap scan is cheaper. Partial index (WHERE status = 'PENDING') should be used instead.
